caption:
Did the Colossus of Rhodes really straddle the harbour? No. That image was a medieval invention.

Rhodes survived a year-long siege by Demetrius I of Macedon. When his army left, the Rhodians sold the abandoned siege equipment for 300 talents and spent the money on a statue of their patron god, Helios. Chares of Lindos worked twelve years. It was finished in 280 BC, about 33 metres tall — the tallest statue in the ancient world.

It stood 54 years. The earthquake of 226 BC snapped it at the knees and it fell onto land. Ptolemy III offered to pay for a rebuild, but the Oracle of Delphi left the Rhodians fearing they had offended Helios, and they declined.

So it lay there for over 800 years, and people travelled to see it broken. Pliny the Elder wrote that few men could get their arms around the thumb, that the fingers were larger than most whole statues, and that where the limbs had broken apart you could see vast caverns yawning inside, with the masses of rock the sculptor used to steady it during construction.

In 653 an Arab force under Mu'awiya I raided Rhodes. Theophanes the Confessor wrote that the bronze was melted down, sold to a merchant of Edessa, and loaded onto 900 camels. Theophanes is the only source for this, and every later version traces back to him; L.I. Conrad considers it likely propaganda.

Still unresolved: where the statue actually stood. Local tradition puts it at the two pillars at the Mandraki port entrance; curved marble blocks in the Fortress of St Nicholas have been proposed as its base; archaeologist Ursula Vedder places it on the acropolis hill instead. Nobody knows its pose either — only that the head had curly hair, like the Helios on Rhodian coins.

Images: engravings by G. de Jode (c. 1580), Antonio Tempesta (1610), Crispijn van de Passe II (1614) and Georg Balthasar Probst (c. 1770); a Rhodian didrachm; and Mandraki harbour today.

cards.note: Theophanes wrote the remains were melted and sold in 653. He is the sole source, and scholars suspect propaganda.

cards.headline: The harbour-straddling pose was <y>a medieval invention</y>
cards.note: Bronze legs held apart would have collapsed under their own weight. No record says he held a torch.

cards.alt: Silver coin showing the head of the sun god Helios facing forward with flowing curly hair.
